Patient Vignette: Mr. K.

Mr. K. is a 74-year-old, retired welder, a slight man with calloused hands and a stillness that feels like held breath. He has been married to his wife, Linh, for 49 years. They live in a quiet suburb, in a house he built with his own hands. He presents for therapy at the urging of his adult daughter, who is concerned about his "moods."

Mr. K. was born in a small coastal village in Vietnam. In 1968, during the Tet Offensive, his village was caught in a crossfire. He was 19, a fisherman's son. He does not speak of the battle itself, but of the aftermath. He describes, in a flat, detached voice, being tasked by the village elders to help gather the dead. For three days, under a brutal sun, he carried bodies-neighbors, a teacher, a young mother he had known since childhood-to a makeshift mass grave. He remembers the heat, the smell, the impossible weight of a child's body in his arms. He remembers the silence after the guns stopped, broken only by the buzzing of flies.

After the war, he fled by boat. He spent two years in a refugee camp in Thailand, a period he describes as a "long wait in a cage." He met Linh there. He came to the United States in 1975, sponsored by a church group. He found work as a welder in a shipyard, a job he held for 40 years. He was good at it. The work was precise, physical, and loud-a noise he could control with his hood and his torch.

Now, in retirement, the silence is a problem.

Mr. K. does not sleep. He lies awake next to Linh, his body rigid, listening. He hears the creak of the house settling and his mind translates it into the snap of a twig under a soldier's boot. He hears a car backfire in the distance and is instantly on his feet, heart hammering, before he even knows he has moved. He has not told Linh about these moments. He simply goes to the kitchen, drinks a glass of water, and stares at the dark window until his hands stop shaking. He feels a deep, corrosive shame about this. A man his age, a grandfather, jumping at shadows.

His world has shrunk. He no longer goes to the Vietnamese community center, where he used to play cards. The crowded room, the rapid-fire chatter, the sudden laughter-it all feels like a pressure on his chest. He cannot tolerate the Fourth of July fireworks. Last year, he spent the entire evening in the basement, sitting on a concrete floor with his hands over his ears, while his grandchildren played above him. He told his daughter he had a headache.

He does not speak of the war. When his son-in-law, a history buff, once asked him about Tet, Mr. K. felt a cold, electric jolt shoot through his spine. He stood up, walked out of the room, and did not return to the dinner table. Later, he told Linh he was "just tired." He is always tired.

The most difficult part, he says, is the feeling of being a ghost. He walks through his own life-the garden he tends, the meals Linh cooks, the grandchildren's drawings on the refrigerator-and feels utterly disconnected from it. He sees his own hands, the ones that built a house and raised a family, and they feel like the hands of a stranger. He sometimes catches his reflection in a window and is surprised to see an old man. Inside, he is still 19, standing in a muddy field, holding a dead child. The smell of jasmine in his garden can suddenly turn, without warning, into the smell of rot and cordite. He will stop, mid-sentence, and go blank for a long moment, his eyes fixed on something no one else can see.

He has come to therapy because his daughter cried. He does not believe it will help. He has spent 55 years trying to forget, and he is terrified that talking about it will only make it more real. He sits in the chair, his hands resting on his knees, perfectly still, as if bracing for an explosion.
